transcript: A bunch of people have asked me how this star-studded production of Tartuffe, led by Matthew Broderick and David Cross compares to the other production of Tartuffe that just finished playing, starring Andre De Shields. And to me the answer is a little bit tricky. This one is directed by Sarah Benson and has a new version of the script by Lucas Hnath. And despite using mostly period costumes and designs, it has a very contemporary feel to it, and not just in the literal language. Even the sense of humor, while still kind of playful and farcical in its own way, also has this wry, off-beat feel to it that comes across very modern in its sensibility. And I would say that vibe is more my personal taste, more my sense of humor. But it didn't really fit the text as well. Like, for example, it made the rhyming verse feel a bit superfluous and even the verse itself felt messier. Like I wasn't even sure if there was a consistent meter or rhyme scheme to it. And while most of these performers individually shined in their roles, it didn't quite feel like a coherent ensemble the way that it did in the Andre De Shields production and the way that I think the text demands. And relatedly, you had some actors who were thriving in the slightly understated, almost naturalistic style of direction, while other actors were thriving despite it. And then a couple other actors Including David Cross, unfortunately, who were not bad by any means, but never quite found their footing amidst the slightly conflicting styles of comedy. And then you have Matthew Broderick, who is not necessarily the best performance in the cast, but is kind of an anchor to the production. He is kind of doing his usual schtick, but it works very well in the role. And it could not be more different from what Andre De Shields was doing. While his Tartuffe was more like the razzle dazzle conman, Matthew Broderick's Tartuffe is kind of a slimy creep who tries to cover that up with a more docile, mild-mannered exterior. Last thing I wanna say is that Lucas Hnath kind of subverts the ending of the story in this production. I won't totally give it away, but I will say, first of all, it involves a song by Heather Christian. Amazing. And it highlights some complicated questions raised by the play's resolution that maybe even Moliere didn't necessarily intend, but that reflect some of the thornier and more uncomfortable truths about our culture today. So even though the production sometimes felt a bit at odds with itself and with the text, Sarah Benson,  Lucas Hnath, and this cast bring a sharp, distinct perspective to it that I really appreciated, both thematically and comedically.
